questions.question: How do you define custom queries in Spring Data MongoDB repositories, and what are the different query mechanisms available?
questions.title: Spring Data MongoDB Repository Queries
questions.direct_answer: Spring Data MongoDB offers four query mechanisms that step up in power and complexity. **Derived query methods** let you express simple filters via method names (`findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter`). **`@Query` annotations** take raw MQL JSON for anything the derived parser can't express (`$or`, `$elemMatch`, nested paths). **`MongoTemplate` with the `Criteria` API** builds queries programmatically for dynamic search forms. The **`Aggregation` API** handles pipelines (`$group`, `$lookup`, `$project`) that the repository layer can't. For reactive apps, swap `MongoRepository` for `ReactiveMongoRepository` to return `Flux` and `Mono`. The skill is knowing when to step down the stack rather than contorting a derived method into something illegible.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the full query toolkit in Spring Data MongoDB and can match mechanism to complexity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using derived methods for every query, leading to 80-character method names; or dropping to `MongoTemplate` for simple queries that a derived method would cover
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the Criteria API for dynamic forms, `MongoTemplate.aggregate()` for pipelines, projection interfaces, and reactive repositories for WebFlux

sections.title: Four Levels of Query Power
sections.content:
Spring Data MongoDB mirrors the Spring Data JPA repository abstraction. `MongoRepository<T, ID>` gives you free CRUD; beyond that, the framework exposes a **layered query system** so you can match the tool to the complexity of the query.

- **Level 1 — Derived methods**: method-name parsing for simple equality and range filters
- **Level 2 — `@Query`**: raw MQL JSON for anything the parser can't express
- **Level 3 — `Criteria` / `Query` via `MongoTemplate`**: programmatic, dynamic query building
- **Level 4 — `Aggregation`**: multi-stage pipelines (`$group`, `$lookup`, `$project`, `$facet`)

Reactive apps swap every level for `ReactiveMongoRepository` and `ReactiveMongoTemplate`, returning `Flux<T>` / `Mono<T>` through the stack on Netty via the MongoDB Reactive Streams driver. Mixing levels is normal — repositories for 80% of reads and `MongoTemplate` for the 20% that are dynamic or pipeline-shaped.

sections.title: Level 1 — Derived Query Methods
Level 2 — `@Query` Annotation
Level 3 — `Criteria` + `MongoTemplate` for Dynamic Queries
Level 4 — `Aggregation` for Pipelines
Reactive Variant
Picking the Right Level
sections.content:
**When derived methods help:**
- Finite, known predicates
- Team wants zero-boilerplate

**When derived methods hurt:**
- Method names bloat past readability
- Cannot express `$or`, `$elemMatch`, `$regex`

**When `@Query` helps:**
- Specific, static, complex MQL that you'd rather write directly

**When Criteria + `MongoTemplate` helps:**
- Dynamic predicates, optional filters
- Programmatic sorting, projection, pagination

**When `Aggregation` is mandatory:**
- Group, join, facet, window — anything pipeline-shaped

**Watch for:**
- N+1 via repositories when `$lookup` would be cheaper
- Derived-method name collisions after refactoring
- `@Query` strings lose IDE refactoring support — consider Criteria when shapes change
- Mixing reactive and blocking templates in the same request path

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four levels**: derived methods, `@Query`, Criteria + `MongoTemplate`, `Aggregation`
- **Use the simplest level that covers the query** — step up only as needed
- **Criteria API** is the go-to for dynamic search forms
- **`MongoTemplate.aggregate()`** handles pipelines that repositories can't express
- **Projection interfaces** reduce payload size for list views
- **Reactive variant** swaps `Mono`/`Flux` through the stack on Netty
- **Transactions** need a replica set and a transaction manager

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Describe the four levels**
- Derived methods — method-name parsing for simple filters
- `@Query` — raw MQL JSON for `$or`, `$elemMatch`, nested paths
- Criteria + `MongoTemplate` — dynamic queries and conditional predicates
- `Aggregation` — pipelines for `$group`, `$lookup`, `$project`, `$facet`

**Give the step-down rule**
- Start with derived; step up only when it becomes illegible or impossible
- Reach for Criteria when predicates depend on runtime input
- Reach for Aggregation when the query is pipeline-shaped

**Mention reactive**
- `ReactiveMongoRepository` + `ReactiveMongoTemplate`
- Non-blocking on Netty

**Close with transactions**
- `MongoTransactionManager` + `@Transactional`
- Requires replica set

questions.question: What are MongoDB change streams and how do you listen to real-time document changes in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: MongoDB Change Streams with Spring Data
questions.direct_answer: **Change streams** are MongoDB's built-in Change Data Capture (CDC) — a resumable, ordered cursor over the oplog that delivers insert/update/replace/delete events to subscribers without polling. They require a **replica set or sharded cluster** (standalone `mongod` cannot emit them). In Spring Boot you listen either **imperatively** with a `MessageListenerContainer` + `ChangeStreamRequest`, or **reactively** with `ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream()` returning `Flux<ChangeStreamEvent<T>>`. The critical operational piece is the **resume token** — store it after each processed event so a restarted consumer picks up where it left off without replay gaps. Common uses include cache invalidation, event-driven microservices, and audit logs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Event-driven integration patterns and understanding of MongoDB's native CDC mechanism
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to run change streams on standalone MongoDB, or not persisting resume tokens — leading to replay gaps on restart
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show `fullDocument: UPDATE_LOOKUP`, resume-token persistence, reactive `changeStream` API, and contrast with Debezium/outbox

sections.title: Change Streams in One Paragraph
sections.content:
A **change stream** is a server-side cursor over MongoDB's oplog filtered to a collection, database, or deployment.
- Your driver reads it like any other cursor and MongoDB pushes events as writes occur — **insert, update, replace, delete, drop, rename, invalidate**.
- Each event carries an `_id` **resume token** so a client that crashes can reopen the stream from exactly the next event.

Change streams need a **replica set or sharded cluster** because the oplog is part of the replication machinery.
- They compose naturally with aggregation — you can `$match` inside the pipeline to filter by operation type, field-level changes, or document shape.
- In Spring you pick between an **imperative `MessageListenerContainer`** and a **reactive `ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream()`**; the reactive API is preferred for modern WebFlux apps because it gives backpressure and integrates with `Flux` pipelines.

sections.title: Change Stream Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    write["Write to collection"] --> oplog["oplog (replica set)"]
    oplog --> cursor["Change stream cursor (filtered pipeline)"]
    cursor --> driver["Reactive driver on Netty"]
    driver --> flux["Flux<ChangeStreamEvent<T>>"]
    flux --> consumer["Consumer (cache invalidator, event publisher, audit log)"]
    consumer --> tokenStore["Persist resume token (Redis/DB)"]
    tokenStore -->|"on restart"| cursor
```

sections.title: Imperative Listener with `MessageListenerContainer`
Reactive Listener with `ReactiveMongoTemplate`
Imperative vs Reactive Change Streams
sections.content:
| Aspect | `MessageListenerContainer` | `ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream()` |
|---|---|---|
| Threading | Dedicated container thread | Netty event loop |
| Backpressure | Manual | Built into `Flux` |
| Fits with | Blocking services, batch | WebFlux, streaming pipelines |
| Restart | Register again + resume | `resumeAt(token)` on subscribe |
| Error handling | Listener callback | `retryWhen`, `onErrorResume` |
| Typical use | Cache invalidation, audit | Event-driven microservices |

sections.title: Operational Notes
sections.content:
**When change streams help:**
- Cache invalidation driven by document writes
- Event-driven microservices without a separate outbox table
- Real-time dashboards and audit logs
- Syncing MongoDB to Elasticsearch / search indexes

**When they hurt:**
- Standalone `mongod` — not supported
- Cross-store CDC with richer semantics — Debezium MongoDB connector is usually better for pipelines into Kafka
- Very high event rates — one consumer can fall behind the oplog retention window

**Watch for:**
- **Oplog retention window** — if your consumer is down longer than the window, the resume token becomes invalid and you get an `invalidate` event
- **`UPDATE_LOOKUP` cost** — each update triggers an extra document fetch; design accordingly
- **Resume-token durability** — persist synchronously with downstream side-effects to avoid duplicate or missed events
- **Multi-consumer semantics** — change streams aren't a queue; each consumer reads independently; use Kafka via Debezium if you need fan-out with retention

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Change streams tail the oplog** — insert, update, replace, delete, plus drop/rename/invalidate
- **Require replica set or sharded cluster** — not supported on standalone
- **Resume tokens** make them resumable; persist them after each event
- **`fullDocument: UPDATE_LOOKUP`** rehydrates post-change document on updates
- **Imperative** via `MessageListenerContainer`; **reactive** via `ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream()`
- **Oplog retention** defines the max safe consumer downtime
- **Use Debezium** for Kafka-based fan-out with longer retention

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**State what they are**
- Server-side resumable cursor over the oplog, filtered per collection/DB/deployment
- Require replica set or sharded cluster

**Show the Spring options**
- Imperative: `MessageListenerContainer` + `ChangeStreamRequest`
- Reactive: `ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream()` returning `Flux<ChangeStreamEvent<T>>`

**Call out `UPDATE_LOOKUP`**
- Needed to get the post-change document on update events
- Costs an extra fetch per event

**Emphasize resume tokens**
- Persist after each processed event
- Drives at-least-once delivery; pair with idempotent handlers

**Close**
- For fan-out with long retention, use Debezium MongoDB connector into Kafka
- Oplog retention window limits safe consumer downtime
